citation.title: Sharp Bounds for Complier Average Potential Outcomes in Experiments with Noncompliance and Incomplete Reporting

standing_assumptions: The work is a three-page letter (Statistics and Probability Letters 83 (2013) 677–679) with one proposition and one corollary, each with a short printed proof, and one application. Everything below was read from the rendered page images (the staged pages, and the staged PDF re-rendered at 260 dpi when this list was fixed). [Setting: Section 2, first paragraph, p. 678 (PDF p. 2)] “We follow the setup of Angrist and Pischke (2009, Chapter 4). Let $Y_i(d, z)$ be the potential outcome of unit $i$ under treatment $d \in \{0, 1\}$ and assignment $z \in \{0, 1\}$, let $D_i(z)$ be the potential treatment of unit $i$ under assignment $z$, and let $Z_i$ be the treatment assigned to unit $i$. The causal effect for unit $i$ is then $Y_i(1, Z_i) - Y_i(0, Z_i)$. We assume (i) random assignment: $[Y_i(d, z), D_i(z) : d, z \in \{0, 1\}] \perp\!\!\!\perp Z_i$; (ii) exclusion restriction: $Y_i(d, z)$ does not depend on $z$, so we may write $Y_i(d, z) = Y_i(d)$; (iii) non-zero first-stage effect: $E[D_i(1) - D_i(0)] \ne 0$; (iv) monotonicity: $\forall i$, $D_i(1) \ge D_i(0)$. We make two notational simplifications. First, given (i), labels are exchangeable and so we drop notational dependence on $i$. Second, we define $P_c \equiv \Pr[D(1) > D(0)]$, $EY_1 \equiv \mathrm{E}[Y|Z = 1]$, and $EY_0 \equiv \mathrm{E}[Y|Z = 0]$.” [LATE display and bounded outcomes: Section 2, second paragraph, p. 678 (PDF p. 2)] “This setting implies that the ``LATE theorem'' (Angrist and Pischke, 2009, Theorem 4.4.1) holds: the CACE, $\mathrm{E}[Y(1) - Y(0)|D(1) > D(0)]$, is equal to $$\frac{\mathrm{E}[Y|Z = 1] - \mathrm{E}[Y|Z = 0]}{\mathrm{E}[D|Z = 1] - \mathrm{E}[D|Z = 0]} = \frac{EY_1 - EY_0}{P_c},$$ where each component may be estimated using sample analogues to population quantities. The associated estimator is logically equivalent to the Wald instrumental variables estimator (Angrist et al., 1996). We make one additional assumption to ensure partial identification: we require that outcomes are bounded. Without loss of generality, fix $Y \in [0, 1]$.” [Typography] The page prints the expectation operator upright in most places ($\mathrm{E}[Y|Z = 1]$) and in italics in assumption (iii) ($E[D_i(1) - D_i(0)]$); it is one operator. $EY_1$, $EY_0$, $EY_n$, $EY_c(0)$, $EY_c(1)$ and $P_c$ are names of real numbers, not products. [What the paper does not print] The paper does not define the observed treatment $D$ and the observed outcome $Y$ that appear in $\mathrm{E}[Y|Z = z]$, $\mathrm{E}[D|Z = z]$, $\mathrm{E}[Y|D = d, Z = z]$ and $\Pr[D = d|Z = z]$ (the relations $D = D(Z)$ and $Y = Y(D(Z))$ are not displayed). It does not say that both assignment arms have positive probability. It does not assume $P_c < 1$: (iii) and (iv) give $0 < P_c \le 1$ only, and ‘two-sided noncompliance’ is stated in Section 4 for the application alone. It does not say whether ‘$Y \in [0, 1]$’ bounds the observed outcome or both potential outcomes. It does not define ‘known’, ‘sharp’, ‘identified’ or ‘point identified’. It has no response or missing-data indicator and no assumption about outcomes that are not recorded. [Remarks for the formalizer, not printed in the paper] The reading the audit's validators settled on is: one probability space (a generic unit) carrying $Z \in \{0,1\}$ with $0 < \Pr[Z = 1] < 1$, potential treatments $D(0), D(1) \in \{0,1\}$ and potential outcomes $Y(0), Y(1) \in [0,1]$ (exclusion is built in: $Y(d,z) = Y(d)$), with $(Y(0), Y(1), D(0), D(1))$ independent of $Z$, $D(1) \ge D(0)$, $\mathrm{E}[D(1) - D(0)] \ne 0$, and observed $D = D(Z)$, $Y = Y(D(Z))$. The unit index is suppressed as generic-unit population notation; the validator of finding P028-N002 (rated a clarity note) established that the printed reason for dropping it (‘given (i), labels are exchangeable’) does not follow from (i) and is not needed, and that no identical-distribution or random-sampling assumption has to be added. Principal strata: compliers $C = \{D(1) > D(0)\} = \{D(0) = 0, D(1) = 1\}$, always-takers $A = \{D(0) = D(1) = 1\}$, never-takers $N = \{D(0) = D(1) = 0\}$; monotonicity excludes $\{D(0) = 1, D(1) = 0\}$, so $D(1) - D(0) = \mathbf{1}_C$, $P_c = \Pr(C) = \mathrm{E}[D(1) - D(0)] = \mathrm{E}[D|Z = 1] - \mathrm{E}[D|Z = 0]$ and $0 < P_c \le 1$; $\Pr(A) = \Pr[D = 1|Z = 0]$, $\Pr(N) = \Pr[D = 0|Z = 1]$ and $\Pr(A) + \Pr(N) = 1 - P_c$. A conditional mean given an event is the elementary one and is defined only when the event has positive probability. Lean's division is total ($x/0 = 0$), so a statement that a printed quotient or conditional mean is undefined has to be stated as the failure of a side condition (a zero denominator, a null conditioning event), not as a property of the quotient's value. Boundedness is used only in Proposition 1; the LATE display and Corollary 1 need integrable outcomes only. [Why the list has ten targets] Three findings rated as errors concern a mathematical statement or rest on an exact formal counterexample. P028-N005 (Moderate): the application presents point estimates of the complier means although 71 of 1000 outcomes are missing and no response assumption is stated; the validator confirmed this with two exact laws that agree on everything observed and disagree on the complier means, so the counterexample (T1), the formal content of the corrected claim (T2) and the passage as printed (T3) are targets. P028-E001 (Minor): a misprinted upper limit and a wrong symbol in the proof of Proposition 1; corrected statement (T4) and the validator's counterexample to the printed intermediate system (T5). P028-E002 (Minor): the proof of Proposition 1 does not cover $P_c = 1$; corrected statement (T6) and the validator's counterexample to the unqualified proof step (T7). The fourth error, P028-E003 (Minor), is a volume number in the reference list and has no mathematical statement to correct. P028-N002 and P028-N007 are clarity notes; P028-N003, P028-N004 and P028-N006 were not confirmed; P028-N001 is undetermined. Of the seven headline claims, H1 (Proposition 1, T8), H3 (Corollary 1, T9) and H2 (the LATE identity and the statement that the three figures do not identify the complier means, T10) are mathematical statements. H4 (the count of 6 of 20 studies), H5 and H6 (the application's estimates) and H7 (the reporting recommendation) are an empirical count, empirical estimates and a recommendation, and are not targets; the formal content behind H6 is reached through P028-N005.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Proof of Proposition 1, ‘Define $EY_n \equiv \mathrm{E}[Y|D(1) = D(0)]$’ and ‘Since $EY_n = [EY_1 - P_c EY_c(1)]/(1 - P_c)$’, used without the condition $P_c < 1$; the witness is the validator's and is not in the paper
canonical_claim.location: p. 678 (PDF p. 2), proof of Proposition 1; the assumptions are in Section 2 on the same page; the related ratio is in the proof of Corollary 1, p. 679 (PDF p. 3)
canonical_claim.statement:
Exact witness (validator's; not in the paper): a model that satisfies every assumption of Section 2 and in which the non-complier group is empty, so that the proof's definition of $EY_n$ conditions on a null event and its division is by $1 - P_c = 0$.
The probability space has two atoms, each of probability $\tfrac12$. Atom 1: $Z = 0$, $D(0) = 0$, $D(1) = 1$, $Y(0) = 0$, $Y(1) = 1$; observed $D = 0$, $Y = 0$. Atom 2: $Z = 1$, $D(0) = 0$, $D(1) = 1$, $Y(0) = 0$, $Y(1) = 1$; observed $D = 1$, $Y = 1$. Here $Y(d, z) = Y(d)$, $D = D(Z)$ and $Y = Y(D)$.
Claims. (F1) The assumptions hold: $(Y(0), Y(1), D(0), D(1))$ is constant, hence independent of $Z$; exclusion holds by the definition of $Y(d,z)$; $D(1) = 1 \ge 0 = D(0)$; $\mathrm{E}[D(1) - D(0)] = 1 \ne 0$; $Y(0), Y(1) \in [0, 1]$; $\Pr[Z = 0] = \Pr[Z = 1] = \tfrac12 > 0$. (F2) $P_c = 1$, $EY_0 = 0$, $EY_1 = 1$, $EY_c(0) = \mathrm{E}[Y(0)|D(1) > D(0)] = 0$ and $EY_c(1) = \mathrm{E}[Y(1)|D(1) > D(0)] = 1$. (F3) $\Pr[D(1) = D(0)] = 0$, $1 - P_c = 0$ and $EY_1 - P_c EY_c(1) = 0$: the conditioning event of $EY_n \equiv \mathrm{E}[Y|D(1) = D(0)]$ has probability zero, and the printed quotient $[EY_1 - P_c EY_c(1)]/(1 - P_c)$ has numerator 0 and denominator 0. (F4) With $P_c = 1$, Eqs. (1) and (2) read $EY_c(0) = EY_0$ and $EY_c(1) = EY_1$ and hold for every real number put in the place of $EY_n$; so Eq. (2) does not determine $EY_n$, and the step ‘Since $EY_n = [EY_1 - P_c EY_c(1)]/(1 - P_c)$’ is not available. (F5) $\Pr[D = 1|Z = 0] = \Pr[D = 0|Z = 1] = 0$: the cells $(D = 1, Z = 0)$ and $(D = 0, Z = 1)$ are empty, $\mathrm{E}[Y|D = 1, Z = 0]$ and $\mathrm{E}[Y|D = 0, Z = 1]$ are conditional means on null events, and the ratio in the proof of Corollary 1 has denominator $\Pr[D = 1|Z = 0] + \Pr[D = 0|Z = 1] = 0$ and, whatever values are assigned to the two empty-cell means (for instance $\tfrac13$ and $\tfrac23$), numerator 0. (F6) The conclusion of Proposition 1 holds in the witness: at $(P_c, EY_0, EY_1) = (1, 0, 1)$ the printed intervals are $[0, 0]$ and $[1, 1]$, which contain $EY_c(0) = 0$ and $EY_c(1) = 1$.
Consequence. The assumptions of Section 2 do not imply $P_c < 1$, and the printed proof of Proposition 1 has no branch for $P_c = 1$; the proposition's intervals are nevertheless correct there (P028-T6). The witness does not satisfy the premise of Corollary 1 on its ordinary reading (two of the four cell means do not exist), so it is not a counterexample to the corollary.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: $EY_n$, $EY_c(0)$, $EY_c(1)$, Eqs. (1)–(2) and the quotient: proof of Proposition 1, p. 678 (PDF p. 2), transcribed in P028-T8. The ratio with denominator $\Pr[D = 1|Z = 0] + \Pr[D = 0|Z = 1]$: proof of Corollary 1, p. 679 (PDF p. 3), transcribed in P028-T9. Assumptions (i)–(iv), $P_c$, $EY_0$, $EY_1$, $Y \in [0, 1]$: Section 2, p. 678, standing assumptions. The two-atom model is the validator's (derivation.md, section 2); in it every unit is a complier. Conditional means are the elementary ones, defined when the conditioning event has positive probability.
canonical_claim.note: Counterexample to the unqualified proof step of a Minor error (P028-E002); priority 3, with its corrected statement P028-T6. The witness is the validator's two-atom model (derivation.md, section 2; exact_check.py and exact_check.out beside it verify (F1)–(F3), (F5) and (F6) with exact fractions and require a zero-denominator exception for each undefined expression); the re-run upheld it. It is a counterexample to a proof step, not to a stated result: Sol's ‘false as printed’ refers to the proof expressions, and no false interval is established. For Lean: division is total there ($0/0 = 0$), and the validator notes that its check does not use ‘Lean's totalized division convention’; the formal content is therefore (F1) and (F2) together with the failed side conditions of (F3) and (F5) (a null conditioning event, a zero denominator), and (F4), which states without any division why the step cannot be carried out. (F4) is this list's rendering of the validator's remark that ‘Even assigning an arbitrary number to a null-group mean cannot license this division’; it is immediate, since $(1 - P_c)\,EY_n = 0$ for every $EY_n$, and was written when this list was fixed. A statement that the quotient ‘equals 0’ or ‘is undefined’ in Lean would not be faithful.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Proposition 1, with its printed proof, Eqs. (1)–(3)
canonical_claim.statement:
[Setting, Section 2, p. 678 (PDF p. 2)] The proposition is stated under the setting of Section 2: assumptions (i) random assignment, (ii) exclusion restriction, (iii) non-zero first-stage effect, (iv) monotonicity, the definitions $P_c \equiv \Pr[D(1) > D(0)]$, $EY_1 \equiv \mathrm{E}[Y|Z = 1]$, $EY_0 \equiv \mathrm{E}[Y|Z = 0]$, and ‘we require that outcomes are bounded. Without loss of generality, fix $Y \in [0, 1]$’ (transcribed in full in the standing assumptions).
[Sentence introducing it, Section 3, p. 678] “Proposition 1 asserts the intervals for complier potential outcomes identified under incomplete reporting.”
[p. 678] Proposition 1. When only $EY_1$, $EY_0$ and $P_c$ are known, sharp bounds exist for the complier average potential outcomes. The average control potential outcome for compliers, $\mathrm{E}[Y(0)|D(1) > D(0)]$ lies in $$\left[\max\left\{0,\ -\frac{EY_1 - EY_0}{P_c},\ 1 - \frac{1 - EY_0}{P_c}\right\},\ \min\left\{1,\ 1 - \frac{EY_1 - EY_0}{P_c},\ \frac{EY_0}{P_c}\right\}\right].$$ Similarly, the average treated potential outcome for compliers, $\mathrm{E}[Y(1)|D(1) > D(0)]$, lies in $$\left[\max\left\{0,\ \frac{EY_1 - EY_0}{P_c},\ 1 - \frac{1 - EY_1}{P_c}\right\},\ \min\left\{1,\ 1 + \frac{EY_1 - EY_0}{P_c},\ \frac{EY_1}{P_c}\right\}\right].$$
[Proof as printed, p. 678] Proof. Define $EY_n \equiv \mathrm{E}[Y|D(1) = D(0)]$, $EY_c(0) \equiv \mathrm{E}[Y(0)|D(1) > D(0)]$ and $EY_c(1) \equiv \mathrm{E}[Y(1)|D(1) > D(0)]$. By the law of total probability, $$P_c EY_c(0) + (1 - P_c)EY_n = EY_0, \qquad (1)$$ $$P_c EY_c(1) + (1 - P_c)EY_n = EY_1, \qquad (2)$$ given the constraints that $0 \le EY_c(0) \le 1$, $0 \le EY_c(1) \le 1$, and $0 \le EY_n \le 1$. Since $EY_n = [EY_1 - P_c EY_c(1)]/(1 - P_c)$, we may reframe the problem as $$P_c EY_c(0) + EY_1 - P_c EY_c(1) = EY_0, \qquad (3)$$ such that $0 \le EY_c(0) \le 1$, $0 \le EY_c(1) \le 1$, and $0 \le EY_1 - P_c EY_c(1) \le 1$. Then substituting the implied value of $EY_c(1)$ from Eq. (3) into the system of inequalities and rearranging terms, we obtain $$0 \le EY_c(1) \le 1,$$ $$(EY_1 - EY_0)/P_c \le EY_c(1) \le 1 + (EY_1 - EY_0)/P_c,$$ $$(EY_1 + P_c - 1)/P_c \le EY_c(1) \le EY_1/P_c,$$ which yields the interval for $EY_c(1)$ asserted by the proposition. The interval for $EY_c(0)$ follows via substitution from the equality in Eq. (3). $\square$
[The hypotheses printed are the setting of Section 2. No condition $P_c < 1$ is printed. The sentence after Eq. (3) is transcribed as printed, with the upper limit 1 and ‘the implied value of $EY_c(1)$’; its corrected form is P028-T4.]
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: [$Y(d)$, $D(z)$, $Z$, assumptions (i)–(iv), $P_c$, $EY_1$, $EY_0$: Section 2, first paragraph, p. 678 (PDF p. 2)] as transcribed in the standing assumptions. [Bounded outcomes: Section 2, second paragraph, p. 678] ‘Without loss of generality, fix $Y \in [0, 1]$.’ [$EY_n$, $EY_c(0)$, $EY_c(1)$: first line of the printed proof, p. 678] $EY_n \equiv \mathrm{E}[Y|D(1) = D(0)]$, $EY_c(0) \equiv \mathrm{E}[Y(0)|D(1) > D(0)]$, $EY_c(1) \equiv \mathrm{E}[Y(1)|D(1) > D(0)]$. [Compliers] the event $D(1) > D(0)$; the paper uses ‘compliers’ and ‘non-compliers’ ($D(1) = D(0)$) without a displayed definition. [Observed $D$, $Y$] not defined in the paper; $D = D(Z)$ and $Y = Y(D(Z))$ on the validators' reading. [‘Known’, ‘sharp bounds’] not defined in the paper; the reading of both fresh readers and the validators is in the note. [The remark after the proof, p. 678] ‘The bounds will tend to be small when (i) the complier average causal effect is close to $-1$ or 1, (ii) average potential outcomes are close to 0 or 1, or (iii) the proportion of compliers is close to 1.’ This is an informal remark and not part of the target.
canonical_claim.note: An exact population statement, so priority 3. The audit's formal reading (both fresh readers and the validators agree on it; it is not printed in this form). Setting: one probability space (a generic unit) carrying $Z \in \{0,1\}$ with $0 < \Pr[Z = 1] < 1$, potential treatments $D(0), D(1) \in \{0,1\}$ and potential outcomes $Y(0), Y(1) \in [0,1]$ (exclusion is built in: $Y(d,z) = Y(d)$), with $(Y(0), Y(1), D(0), D(1))$ independent of $Z$, $D(1) \ge D(0)$, $\mathrm{E}[D(1) - D(0)] \ne 0$, and observed $D = D(Z)$, $Y = Y(D(Z))$. Write $p = P_c$, $e_z = EY_z$, $\tau = (e_1 - e_0)/p$, $c_d = \mathrm{E}[Y(d)|D(1) > D(0)]$, and let $[L_0, U_0]$, $[L_1, U_1]$ be the two printed intervals. Validity: in every such model $L_0 \le c_0 \le U_0$ and $L_1 \le c_1 \le U_1$; moreover $c_1 = c_0 + \tau$, $L_1 = L_0 + \tau$ and $U_1 = U_0 + \tau$. Sharpness (‘when only $EY_1$, $EY_0$ and $P_c$ are known’): for all real $p \in (0, 1]$ and $e_0, e_1 \in [0, 1]$ with $|e_1 - e_0| \le p$, and every $x_1 \in [L_1, U_1]$, there is a model satisfying the setting with $(P_c, EY_0, EY_1) = (p, e_0, e_1)$, $c_1 = x_1$ and $c_0 = x_1 - \tau$; so every point of each interval, endpoints included, is attained, and no narrower interval is valid. The triples with $|e_1 - e_0| \le p$ are exactly those that arise from some model and exactly those for which the printed intervals are nonempty (the re-run of P028-E002 obtains the equivalent condition $\max\{0, e_0 - p, e_1 - p\} \le m \le \min\{1 - p, e_0, e_1\}$ on the non-complier contribution; the equivalence was checked when this list was fixed). Attaining models (validators' construction): if $p < 1$, a fraction $p$ of compliers with constant potential outcomes $(x_1 - \tau, x_1)$ and a fraction $1 - p$ of never-takers with both potential outcomes equal to $(e_1 - p\,x_1)/(1 - p)$, with $Z$ an independent fair coin; if $p = 1$, compliers only, with constant potential outcomes $(e_0, e_1)$. The proposition does not fix the split of non-compliers into always-takers and never-takers, so a model with never-takers only is permitted. The printed proof gives the validity half; the attainability half is left implicit, and its sentence after Eq. (3) and its treatment of $P_c = 1$ are the subjects of findings P028-E001 and P028-E002 (both Minor): the corrected steps are P028-T4 and P028-T6 and the counterexamples to the printed steps are P028-T5 and P028-T7. Neither finding changes the statement: both validators established that the two intervals are correct and sharp for every $P_c \in (0, 1]$. A complete derivation with no division by $1 - P_c$ is sections 3–4 of the artifact named here; the batch validator's derivation for $0 < P_c < 1$ is the docstring of validate/_batch/P028-B01/work/check_math.py. ‘Without loss of generality’ for $Y \in [0, 1]$ is a normalization of a bounded outcome; for the formal statement boundedness of both potential outcomes in $[0, 1]$ is an assumption. The unit index and the phrase ‘labels are exchangeable’ are the subject of P028-N002 (a clarity note): the generic-unit reading above needs no added assumption. Worked instances, recomputed in exact arithmetic when this list was fixed: the application's inputs $(P_c, EY_0, EY_1) = (21/100, 45/100, 51/100)$ give $[0, 5/7]$ and $[2/7, 1]$ (printed $[0, 0.71]$ and $[0.29, 1]$, p. 679); $(3/5, 83/300, 173/300)$ gives $[0, 83/180]$ and $[1/2, 173/180]$; $(1/2, 3/4, 3/4)$ gives $[1/2, 1]$ twice; $(1, e_0, e_1)$ gives $\{e_0\}$ and $\{e_1\}$. Both fresh readers report that the claim held up, with the caveats about the proof recorded above.

canonical_claim.statement:
[Setting, Section 2, p. 678 (PDF p. 2)] The corollary is stated under the setting of Section 2: assumptions (i)–(iv) and the definitions of $P_c$, $EY_1$, $EY_0$ (transcribed in full in the standing assumptions).
[Sentence introducing it, p. 678] “For contrast, we state sufficient conditions for point identification in Corollary 1, following the well-known result in, e.g., Imbens and Rubin (1997).”
[p. 678] Corollary 1. If $\mathrm{E}[Y|D = d, Z = z]$ and $\Pr[D = d|Z = z]$, for $d, z \in \{0, 1\}$, are known, the complier average potential outcomes are point identified. $\mathrm{E}[Y(0)|D(1) > D(0)]$ is equal to $$\frac{EY_0 - \Pr[D = 1|Z = 0]\,\mathrm{E}[Y|D = 1, Z = 0] - \Pr[D = 0|Z = 1]\,\mathrm{E}[Y|D = 0, Z = 1]}{P_c}$$ and $\mathrm{E}[Y(1)|D(1) > D(0)] = \mathrm{E}[Y(0)|D(1) > D(0)] + (EY_1 - EY_0)/P_c$.
[Proof as printed, p. 679 (PDF p. 3)] Proof. The average outcome for non-compliers, $\mathrm{E}[Y|D(1) = D(0)]$, is equal to $$\frac{\Pr[D = 1|Z = 0]\,\mathrm{E}[Y|D = 1, Z = 0] + \Pr[D = 0|Z = 1]\,\mathrm{E}[Y|D = 0, Z = 1]}{\Pr[D = 1|Z = 0] + \Pr[D = 0|Z = 1]}.$$ Substitution of $\mathrm{E}[Y|D(1) = D(0)]$ into Eqs. (1) and (2) yields the result. $\square$
[The hypotheses printed are the setting of Section 2 and the premise that $\mathrm{E}[Y|D = d, Z = z]$ and $\Pr[D = d|Z = z]$ are known for $d, z \in \{0, 1\}$. Eqs. (1) and (2) are those of the proof of Proposition 1, transcribed in P028-T8.]
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: [$Y(d)$, $D(z)$, $Z$, assumptions (i)–(iv), $P_c$, $EY_1$, $EY_0$: Section 2, p. 678 (PDF p. 2)] as transcribed in the standing assumptions. [Eqs. (1), (2) and $EY_n \equiv \mathrm{E}[Y|D(1) = D(0)]$: proof of Proposition 1, p. 678] $P_c EY_c(0) + (1 - P_c)EY_n = EY_0$ and $P_c EY_c(1) + (1 - P_c)EY_n = EY_1$. [$\mathrm{E}[Y|D = d, Z = z]$, $\Pr[D = d|Z = z]$] not defined beyond the notation: the elementary conditional mean of the observed outcome in the cell where observed treatment is $d$ and assignment is $z$, defined when the cell has positive probability, and the conditional probability of observed treatment $d$ given assignment $z$. [Observed $D$, $Y$] not defined in the paper; $D = D(Z)$, $Y = Y(D(Z))$ on the validators' reading. [‘Known’, ‘point identified’] not defined in the paper; read by the fresh readers and the validator as: each complier mean equals an expression in the law of the observed $(Y, D, Z)$ alone, which the two displayed formulas are ($EY_0$, $EY_1$ and $P_c = \Pr[D = 1|Z = 1] - \Pr[D = 1|Z = 0]$ are themselves functions of the eight ‘known’ quantities).
canonical_claim.note: An exact population identity, so priority 3. The audit's formal reading (section 5 of the artifact named here; not printed in this form). Setting: one probability space (a generic unit) carrying $Z \in \{0,1\}$ with $0 < \Pr[Z = 1] < 1$, potential treatments $D(0), D(1) \in \{0,1\}$ and potential outcomes $Y(0), Y(1) \in [0,1]$ (exclusion is built in: $Y(d,z) = Y(d)$), with $(Y(0), Y(1), D(0), D(1))$ independent of $Z$, $D(1) \ge D(0)$, $\mathrm{E}[D(1) - D(0)] \ne 0$, and observed $D = D(Z)$, $Y = Y(D(Z))$, except that bounded outcomes are not needed (integrable potential outcomes suffice). Write $q = \Pr[D = 1|Z = 0]$, $r = \Pr[D = 0|Z = 1]$, $\mu_{10} = \mathrm{E}[Y|D = 1, Z = 0]$, $\mu_{01} = \mathrm{E}[Y|D = 0, Z = 1]$. Premise on the ordinary reading: the four cell means exist, that is, every cell $(D = d, Z = z)$ has positive probability; given the setting this is $q > 0$ and $r > 0$ (two-sided noncompliance), which forces $P_c < 1$. Conclusions: (a) $q = \Pr(A)$, $r = \Pr(N)$ and $P_c = 1 - q - r$, where $A$ and $N$ are the always-takers and never-takers; (b) $\mu_{10} = \mathrm{E}[Y(1)|A]$ and $\mu_{01} = \mathrm{E}[Y(0)|N]$; (c) the proof's display: $\mathrm{E}[Y|D(1) = D(0)] = (q\,\mu_{10} + r\,\mu_{01})/(q + r)$; (d) $\mathrm{E}[Y(0)|D(1) > D(0)] = (EY_0 - q\,\mu_{10} - r\,\mu_{01})/P_c$; (e) $\mathrm{E}[Y(1)|D(1) > D(0)] = \mathrm{E}[Y(0)|D(1) > D(0)] + (EY_1 - EY_0)/P_c = (EY_1 - q\,\mu_{10} - r\,\mu_{01})/P_c$. Finding P028-E002 (Minor) touches the proof, not the statement: the validator confirmed that the ratio in (c) cannot be carried to models with an empty cell (its denominator $q + r = 1 - P_c$ vanishes at full compliance, P028-T7), and found the corollary valid under its premise; the product-moment form that needs no positivity of cells is P028-T6 (v), an optional extension. Under one-sided noncompliance (exactly one of $q$, $r$ zero) the premise fails on the ordinary reading; the Opus fresh reader reports the formula exact on 4000 random models including one-sided cases and $P_c = 1$ when terms with zero probability are read as 0, which is the content of P028-T6 (v). The citation ‘Imbens and Rubin (1997)’ is the subject of P028-E003 (a volume number in the reference list; not a target). The application of this formula to incompletely recorded outcomes in Section 4 is the subject of P028-N005 (P028-T1 to P028-T3) and does not touch the corollary as a statement about the full joint law. Worked instance, from the re-run of P028-E002 and recomputed when this list was fixed: $p = 3/5$, $e_0 = 83/300$, $e_1 = 173/300$, non-complier contribution $q\,\mu_{10} + r\,\mu_{01} = 19/150$ give complier means $1/4$ and $3/4$. Both fresh readers report that the claim held up (one with the empty-cell caveat).

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: The ‘LATE theorem’ display of Section 2 (unnumbered), with the Introduction's statement that the three reported figures do not identify the average potential outcomes for compliers
canonical_claim.location: p. 678 (PDF p. 2), Section 2, second paragraph; p. 677 (PDF p. 1), Section 1, first paragraph
canonical_claim.statement:
[Setting, Section 2, first paragraph, p. 678 (PDF p. 2)] “We follow the setup of Angrist and Pischke (2009, Chapter 4). Let $Y_i(d, z)$ be the potential outcome of unit $i$ under treatment $d \in \{0, 1\}$ and assignment $z \in \{0, 1\}$, let $D_i(z)$ be the potential treatment of unit $i$ under assignment $z$, and let $Z_i$ be the treatment assigned to unit $i$. The causal effect for unit $i$ is then $Y_i(1, Z_i) - Y_i(0, Z_i)$. We assume (i) random assignment: $[Y_i(d, z), D_i(z) : d, z \in \{0, 1\}] \perp\!\!\!\perp Z_i$; (ii) exclusion restriction: $Y_i(d, z)$ does not depend on $z$, so we may write $Y_i(d, z) = Y_i(d)$; (iii) non-zero first-stage effect: $E[D_i(1) - D_i(0)] \ne 0$; (iv) monotonicity: $\forall i$, $D_i(1) \ge D_i(0)$. We make two notational simplifications. First, given (i), labels are exchangeable and so we drop notational dependence on $i$. Second, we define $P_c \equiv \Pr[D(1) > D(0)]$, $EY_1 \equiv \mathrm{E}[Y|Z = 1]$, and $EY_0 \equiv \mathrm{E}[Y|Z = 0]$.”
[Section 2, second paragraph, p. 678] “This setting implies that the ``LATE theorem'' (Angrist and Pischke, 2009, Theorem 4.4.1) holds: the CACE, $\mathrm{E}[Y(1) - Y(0)|D(1) > D(0)]$, is equal to $$\frac{\mathrm{E}[Y|Z = 1] - \mathrm{E}[Y|Z = 0]}{\mathrm{E}[D|Z = 1] - \mathrm{E}[D|Z = 0]} = \frac{EY_1 - EY_0}{P_c},$$ where each component may be estimated using sample analogues to population quantities.”
[Section 1, first paragraph, p. 677 (PDF p. 1)] “When reporting results from experiments with noncompliance, including encouragement designs, researchers often include estimates of the average outcomes in treatment, average outcomes in control and the difference in average take-up between assignment statuses. These figures are sufficient for estimating a complier average causal effect (CACE), sometimes referred to as a local average treatment effect (Angrist et al., 1996). Although sufficient information is typically estimable from the data (Imbens and Rubin, 1997), these three figures alone do not provide enough information to identify the average potential outcomes for compliers.”
[The hypotheses printed for the display are the setting of Section 2, assumptions (i)–(iv). The bounded-outcome assumption is introduced after the display and is not attached to it.]
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: [$Y(d)$, $D(z)$, $Z$, assumptions (i)–(iv), $P_c$, $EY_1$, $EY_0$: Section 2, first paragraph, p. 678 (PDF p. 2)] as transcribed in the statement. [CACE] ‘complier average causal effect (CACE), sometimes referred to as a local average treatment effect’ (Section 1, p. 677); in Section 2 it is $\mathrm{E}[Y(1) - Y(0)|D(1) > D(0)]$. [$\mathrm{E}[D|Z = z]$] the mean of the observed treatment given assignment; the observed $D$ and $Y$ are not defined in the paper ($D = D(Z)$, $Y = Y(D(Z))$ on the validators' reading). [‘These three figures’] the average outcomes of units assigned to treatment and to control and the difference in average take-up between assignment statuses (Section 1, p. 677; abstract, p. 677), that is, $EY_1$, $EY_0$ and $\mathrm{E}[D|Z = 1] - \mathrm{E}[D|Z = 0] = P_c$. [‘Identify’] not defined in the paper. The cited theorem (Angrist and Pischke 2009, Theorem 4.4.1) is not staged and is not needed: the display follows from the setting.
canonical_claim.note: An exact population identity and a non-identification statement, so priority 3. No finding rated as an error concerns it; P028-N002 (the sentence on exchangeable labels) is a clarity note and the generic-unit reading needs no added assumption. The audit's formal reading (not printed in this form). Setting: one probability space (a generic unit) carrying $Z \in \{0,1\}$ with $0 < \Pr[Z = 1] < 1$, potential treatments $D(0), D(1) \in \{0,1\}$ and potential outcomes $Y(0), Y(1) \in [0,1]$ (exclusion is built in: $Y(d,z) = Y(d)$), with $(Y(0), Y(1), D(0), D(1))$ independent of $Z$, $D(1) \ge D(0)$, $\mathrm{E}[D(1) - D(0)] \ne 0$, and observed $D = D(Z)$, $Y = Y(D(Z))$, except that bounded outcomes are not needed (integrable potential outcomes suffice). (a) First stage: $\mathrm{E}[D|Z = 1] - \mathrm{E}[D|Z = 0] = \mathrm{E}[D(1) - D(0)] = \Pr[D(1) > D(0)] = P_c$, and $P_c > 0$. (b) Reduced form: $\mathrm{E}[Y|Z = 1] - \mathrm{E}[Y|Z = 0] = P_c \cdot \mathrm{E}[Y(1) - Y(0)|D(1) > D(0)]$. (c) Hence the display: $\mathrm{E}[Y(1) - Y(0)|D(1) > D(0)] = (EY_1 - EY_0)/P_c$, with a nonzero denominator. (a) is section 1 of the artifact named here and (b) is the difference of the two mixture equations $e_z = p\,c_z + m$ of its section 3 (P028-T6 (ii)); both fresh readers verified the identity independently. (d) Non-identification of the levels: there are two models satisfying the setting with bounded outcomes that have the same $(P_c, EY_0, EY_1)$ and different complier means. Exact witness (the Sol fresh reader's check of this claim, built with the validators' attaining construction of P028-T8, and recomputed when this list was fixed): for each $t \in [\tfrac12, 1]$ take a fraction $\tfrac12$ of compliers with $Y(0) = Y(1) = t$ and a fraction $\tfrac12$ of never-takers with $Y(0) = Y(1) = \tfrac32 - t$, with $Z$ an independent fair coin; then $P_c = \tfrac12$, $EY_0 = EY_1 = \tfrac34$ and the CACE is 0 for every $t$, while both complier means equal $t$. The models $t = \tfrac12$ and $t = 1$ are such a pair. The paper's ‘do not provide enough information to identify’ is a general statement: at some triples the levels are identified (at $P_c = 1$, P028-T6 (vii); more generally whenever the intervals of Proposition 1 are single points), so the formal statement is existential, as in (d), and not ‘for every triple’. The estimation clause (‘may be estimated using sample analogues’, ‘logically equivalent to the Wald instrumental variables estimator’) is not part of the target.
